title: China Voices 'Serious Concern' Over New US Curbs Ahead of Xi-Trump Summit, Water Cyberattacks Hit Seven States
subhead: Beijing pushes back on escalating tech restrictions days after Bessent-He call, as suspected Iranian cyberattacks on US water systems expand and the AI industry confronts a circular financing reckoning that wiped $1.3 trillion from chip stocks last week.

sections.heading: China Pushes Back on US Tech Curbs Ahead of Xi-Trump Summit
sections.body:
China expressed 'serious concern' over recent US economic and trade restrictions during a video call between Vice-Premier He Lifeng, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, according to Xinhua's readout. The call came as both sides prepare economic deliverables for Xi Jinping's expected visit to the US in September.

The restrictions prompting Beijing's objection include the Trump administration's ban on Chinese robots and power inverters (via an FCC Covered List expansion last Tuesday), fresh Section 301 tariffs on China and 59 other economies, and an ongoing investigation into excess industrial capacity across 16 economies. Bessent said he expected Beijing to 'fully meet its commitments on rare earths and US agricultural products.'

The tension is real and growing even as diplomacy continues. USTR Greer told the Senate Finance Committee that Washington is still 'not getting enough' critical mineral exports from China, whose rare earth shipments to the US fell 22.5% year-on-year in January and February despite a truce reached in Busan last year. Both sides are simultaneously negotiating and escalating — a pattern that has defined the relationship since the first tariff rounds but is now extending deeper into technology controls, rare earths, and AI model access.
sections.whyItMatters: The Xi-Trump September summit is supposed to deliver trade outcomes, but each side is layering on new restrictions faster than they can negotiate the old ones. The board-of-trade mechanism (capped at $30 billion each in tariff-free trade) and rare earths flows are the test cases for whether managed decoupling can coexist with managed interdependence.

sections.heading: Water System Cyberattacks Spread to Seven States and Canada
sections.body:
FBI and EPA investigations are ongoing after cyberattacks hit water utilities in at least seven US states — including over 30 community water systems in Minnesota and nine in Michigan — with systems in South Dakota and others also affected. CISA confirmed a 'significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector,' with hackers modifying passwords to lock operators out and changing IP addresses on affected controllers.

Intelligence officials have pointed to Iranian-linked actors as the likely source, though no formal attribution has been made on the record. The mayor of Braham, Minnesota, Nate George, said state and federal investigators privately believe 'it's Iranian actors.' President Trump, however, publicly rejected that assessment, telling a Camp David cabinet meeting: 'I think that Minnesota is behind it... I don't think there was an Iranian cyberattack.' Minnesota Governor Tim Walz fired back, blaming DOGE-era cuts to CISA for leaving the US 'exposed to cyber attacks.'

In Canada, the small Quebec municipality of Saint-Noël was targeted by a separate attack traced to Z-Pentest Alliance, a Russian-linked group. The hackers posted video of themselves adjusting chlorine dosage settings; the plant went into safe mode and water was not contaminated. CISA had already warned in 2025 that pro-Russia hacktivist groups were conducting opportunistic attacks on critical infrastructure globally.
sections.whyItMatters: Two separate state-linked cyber campaigns targeting water infrastructure on the same continent in the same week — one suspected Iranian, one attributed to a Russian military-intelligence-linked group — turns municipal water systems from a theoretical vulnerability into an active target. The political disagreement over attribution in Washington complicates the response.

sections.heading: AI's Circular Financing Problem Erupts as Chip Stocks Shed $1.3 Trillion
sections.body:
The week ending August 1 was the roughest for chip stocks in years. Chip equities shed $1.3 trillion in value across global markets. South Korea's Kospi fell 11.5% on Tuesday and another 6% on Wednesday — its worst month since October 2008 — dragged down by SK Hynix and Samsung. Nvidia dropped nearly 5% in a single session before a partial rebound on strong Amazon and Microsoft earnings.

The trigger was not a demand collapse. Alphabet reported 82% cloud growth and raised capex to as much as $205 billion — and still got sold. The problem is structural, as analyst firm Morningstar framed it: a 'loss of confidence' in the specific business model, not in AI itself. The four largest US tech firms are on course to spend $725 billion on infrastructure this year, up 77% from 2025, yet free cash flow at Google turned negative for the quarter.

The circular financing dynamic crystallized further when the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia is considering a $250 billion backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio, six months after a previous $100 billion deal between the two fell apart. AMD invested $5 billion in Anthropic, which then uses AMD chips. As Bloomberg's Dina Bass reported on NPR, 'a company giving another company money to buy its product' is now a defining feature of the AI economy. Wedbush flagged near-term risks from Nvidia's alleged OpenAI data center support. Analysts at RealClearMarkets argued the premium for being first with the best model 'is finished,' as open-weight rivals like Moonshot's Kimi K3 now match closed leaders on benchmarks at a fraction of the cost.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is repricing the AI infrastructure buildout not because AI doesn't work, but because the returns are lagging the spending by a widening margin. If Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta report earnings this week that don't narrow the gap between capex and cash returns, the selloff extends — and the $800 billion+ in circular financing tying Nvidia, OpenAI, CoreWeave, and AMD together amplifies every disappointment.

sections.heading: DeepSeek Plans 1 GW Data Center in Inner Mongolia
sections.body:
DeepSeek is planning a gigawatt-scale AI data center in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, according to a Bloomberg report. The facility would add at least 1 GW of computing capacity roughly 350 km northwest of Beijing, with part of the campus built by DeepSeek and part leased from existing operators. At least some capacity could come online by end of 2027 or early 2028.

Ulanqab is already an established computing cluster — Apple, Alibaba, and Huawei have data center infrastructure there. The city's cold climate allows natural cooling for up to 10 months per year, and China connected a green-powered computing base in the region in July 2025, combining 200 MW of wind, 100 MW of solar, and 45 MW of energy storage.

The processor mix remains the politically sensitive unknown. A senior US official told Reuters in February that DeepSeek trained an advanced model using Nvidia Blackwell processors despite export restrictions, with chips likely clustered at a data center in Inner Mongolia. DeepSeek has not confirmed this. The company could use Nvidia hardware, Huawei processors, its own future chips, or a combination. Reuters also reported that DeepSeek is developing its own custom chips.
sections.whyItMatters: DeepSeek built its reputation on doing more with less. A 1 GW facility signals a shift from efficiency to scale — and from software independence to hardware sovereignty. If the Blackwell allegation is accurate, it also raises hard questions about how effectively export controls prevent advanced chips from reaching Chinese AI companies.

sections.heading: Chinese Military Researchers Tap US AI Models for Defense Systems
sections.body:
A Reuters investigation published July 31 found that Chinese military and security-linked institutions are using American AI models — including open-weight systems released by US companies — to train defense systems. The previously unreported findings offer a rare glimpse into how models designed for civilian use are being repurposed for military applications in China, according to the report.

The finding lands amid an intensifying debate in Washington about whether to restrict the release of open-weight AI models. Anthropic has argued publicly that advanced Chinese open-weight models represent a national security threat, while a coalition of 150 companies backed open-weight AI in late July. The Reuters reporting complicates the open-weight camp's case: it's not just Chinese-origin models that pose a risk, but also American-origin open models that can be downloaded and adapted by any actor, including military ones.
sections.whyItMatters: The open-weight debate in Washington has focused on whether Chinese models like DeepSeek and Kimi should be restricted from US download. The Reuters finding flips the direction: American open models are already being used by China's military. That's a harder problem to solve with export controls, since the models are already publicly available.

sections.heading: CXMT Nears LPDDR6 Production, DUV Lithography Ceiling Reveals the Gap
sections.body:
CXMT, the Chinese memory chipmaker whose $8.6 billion IPO rattled global markets last week, is nearing LPDDR6 production validation — but at a design speed of 12,800 Mbps, roughly 11% below the 14,400 Mbps standard achieved by Samsung and SK Hynix. The gap reflects the ceiling imposed by China's domestic DUV lithography, which cannot yet match ASML's precision.

The broader memory chip market remains in shortage. Samsung warned investors that memory shortages will worsen through 2027, with no real relief expected before 2028. SK Hynix and Micron also face supply constraints. Forrester analyst Alvin Nguyen called the sell-off in memory stocks an 'overreaction,' noting that global demand continues to outstrip supply — CXMT is adding capacity but not yet at the performance frontier needed to displace the incumbents.
sections.whyItMatters: CXMT's LPDDR6 is close enough to compete on price in commodity markets but still behind on performance — the DUV gap is 11%, not 0%. For China's domestic chip strategy, that's real progress. For the incumbents, it's a warning that the price-undercutting playbook China used in steel and autos is now arriving in memory chips, even if the premium tier remains protected for now.

sections.heading: Türkiye: NATO Summit Outcomes and Defense Tech Trajectory
sections.body:
The 2026 NATO Summit in Ankara (July 7-8) focused heavily on defense production, investment, and innovation, with Türkiye positioning itself as an increasingly important defense-industrial player within the alliance. Discussions covered defense industry cooperation, technology transfer, and the role of allied manufacturing in sustaining the Ukraine conflict and deterring further aggression.

Türkiye's defense exports have been growing steadily, with Baykar drones and ASELSAN electronics finding markets beyond their traditional buyers. The summit outcomes reinforced Ankara's dual role: a NATO member with deepening indigenous defense-tech capabilities and a country that maintains independent relationships with both Western and non-Western arms customers.
sections.whyItMatters: Türkiye's defense tech trajectory — particularly in drones, electronic warfare, and indigenous radar — positions it as a middle-power exporter whose products are battle-tested and priced below Western equivalents. The Ankara summit crystallized how defense-industrial capacity is becoming a form of geopolitical leverage within NATO itself.

bottomLine: Three dynamics collided this week: Beijing formally protested escalating US tech restrictions days before a summit designed to ease tensions, suspected state-linked cyberattacks on water infrastructure expanded across North America while the US president publicly rejected his own intelligence community's attribution, and the AI infrastructure economy hit a financial reckoning point where $725 billion in annual spending is being questioned by markets that no longer believe frontier model dominance is a durable moat. None of these are resolved — the Xi-Trump summit, the FBI investigation, and this week's Big Tech earnings will each shape what comes next.
sources: South China Morning Post, The Guardian, NPR, Bloomberg via NPR, Reuters, CBC, International Business Times, RealClearMarkets, Memeburn, TweakTown, Forbes, CNBC, Morningstar, Wall Street Journal, USA Today, CISA, Xinhua, SCMP, Khan (Korean Herald), Yahoo News
